title: Gurdwaras abroad
hook: great gurdwaras stand in London, Toronto, Nairobi, Kuala Lumpur

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hemkunt Sahib, the cold lake and the poem of a calling. Your line was the high lake. Did you carry one still breath through a busy door? Day one thousand three hundred forty-one.

Where does a Guru live, when the family moves across the world? Try a wet London street, buses going by, a row of shops, and then a building with a dome and a tall saffron flag out front. A wide suburban road outside Toronto, a parking lot full on a Sunday morning. A gurdwara in Nairobi, its doors open to the morning traffic. A gurdwara in Kuala Lumpur, with shoes lined up at the door in the heat. Different weather, different streets, and inside each of them, the same thing at the center: the Guru Granth Sahib, on a raised seat, under a canopy.
screen: `LONDON, TORONTO.` → `NAIROBI, KUALA LUMPUR.` → `THE SAME THING AT THE CENTER.`

segments.voice: First, what makes a gurdwara. It isn't the dome or the city. Sikhs say the Guru Granth Sahib is the Guru, so wherever it is installed with respect, on a raised seat, opened each morning and put to rest at night, that place is the Guru's court, the darbar. A gurdwara in Toronto is not a copy of a gurdwara in Punjab. It's the same Guru, in a new place. Second, the Guru's word on this. Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, writes, in paraphrase: wherever my True Guru goes and sits, that place is beautiful. Some Sikhs far from Punjab hear their own story in that line. The Guru goes where the sangat goes. Third, the two signs you can spot from the street. The Nishan Sahib, the tall flag, marks a gurdwara from a distance. And the langar marks it from the inside: a free kitchen where anyone may sit and eat, Sikh or not. Those two travel well. Fourth, what else grew in these buildings. For families who moved far from home, the gurdwara became more than a place to pray. It's where weddings happen, where children learn Gurmukhi letters on weekends, where newcomers find someone who speaks their language, and where a stranger can get a hot meal. In London, Toronto, Nairobi and Kuala Lumpur, the details differ: the food, the accents, the weather at the door. The seat at the center is the same.
screen: `WHERE THE GRANTH SITS, THE GURU SITS.` · `WHEREVER MY TRUE GURU SITS.` · `THE FLAG AND THE KITCHEN.` · `MORE THAN A PLACE TO PRAY.` · then, large: `THE GURU ABROAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look one up. That comes after the bell. For now, settle, and breathe. Think of the town or city where you live, or one you love. Picture its streets. Somewhere among them, maybe, is a saffron flag you've walked past without noticing. Picture the door, the shoes lined up, the smell of the kitchen. Then, when the bell rings, look up the gurdwara nearest you, or in a city you'd like to visit, and read one thing about it. The bell holds the time.
Gurdwaras abroad. Sikh houses of the Guru far from Punjab, in London, Toronto, Nairobi, Kuala Lumpur and beyond, each one the Guru's court because the Guru Granth Sahib is there. Today's word.
Your line: the guru abroad. Today, when you pass a place of worship that isn't familiar to you, look at it a little longer, and wonder who keeps it. Day one thousand three hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Sikhs around the world gather at local gurdwaras, where the Guru Granth Sahib is installed, kirtan is sung, and the langar serves a free meal to anyone who comes.
